\textbf{Accuracy on instructed-lie benchmarks does not identify deception: the intervention that creates the lie also changes instruction-following behavior.} Such benchmarks are validated by predictive accuracy, not by construct identification. We introduce an identification audit for them, and show that the common instructed-lie paradigm fails it. \textbf{We do not ask whether LLMs can detect deception; we ask whether current benchmarks provide evidence that they do.} The standard paradigm scores detectors in one setting, \emph{instructed roleplay}, so a detector can score high while measuring whether the model was \emph{instructed} to lie. The reason is structural: \textbf{no experiment that intervenes only on the instruction can separate a detector response mediated by deception from one mediated by instruction-following}, both being descendants of that instruction. A deception-attribution reading therefore needs $\tau_D$, the effect of \emph{deception}, which the identified $\tau_E$---the \emph{instruction}'s effect---neither bounds nor signs, so no gain in accuracy, scale, or detector sophistication resolves it. \textbf{This is an identification problem, not a generalization problem: generalization can be perfect while identification still fails.} We turn it into a falsifiable audit protocol: a five-part identification audit---\textbf{one necessary construct-validity test no instructed design can supply}, plus three alternative-explanation diagnostics and one robustness test. Fixed elicitation itself is not new---trained belief-verified organisms have it---but it has not been used as the \emph{construct-validity criterion} for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy.

Reimplemented from scratch, the standard black-box behavioral detector reaches 81.7\% on instructed-lie trials and 53.7\% once both conditions receive identical prompts. A pre-registered replication on a disjoint claim set and probe bank then \textbf{leaves no detectable above-chance discrimination on any of the six targets} (97.0\%$\to$\textbf{43.3\%}), as does a white-box linear probe on residual activations in two model families, at 100.0\% instructed, at chance equalized, and matched by surface features (92.5--99.0\%). \textbf{The accuracy the benchmark is scored on is reachable with no learned features at all}: a parameter-free lexical rule reaches 69--80\%---\emph{surface-accessible accuracy}, not a decomposition of the detector's signal. We then audit both public rollout releases for the one criterion that removes the elicitation confound: \textbf{nine of ten rollout sets cannot supply it} for a deployed-observable rule; on the tenth our rule is \textbf{null} while \textbf{the corpus authors' own judge, run verbatim on the same visible text, does separate deception there} (AUROC 0.71/0.94), so the null is the instrument's, not the criterion's; scoring the \emph{hidden} scaffold instead reports $+84.3$\,pp---\textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, the model echoing ``incorrect'' from its own instruction. A second release---35 cells, five generator families, fully pre-registered---fails differently: its label grades the very text both instruments read, so passing is \textbf{construct recovery}. We claim identification, not attribution, and \textbf{equalization may remove the deception with the confound}. Because \textbf{no public release we audited supplies all five}, we built materials that do: with deception operationalized independently of the detector's input, prior work's battery separates operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three with power ($p\!\leq\!0.006$; two underpowered nulls)---of which \textbf{a blinded re-run replicates two and a pre-registered covariate audit then withdraws one of those two, so the standing count is one of five}, with \textbf{one of five \emph{new} targets positive}. \textbf{The audit also changes \emph{which} probe indicates deception}: the instructed benchmark's most discriminative question is inert at fixed elicitation. \textbf{The canonical benchmark fails to identify deception, while a fixed-elicitation design reveals \emph{target-dependent} deception-associated signals}---still not $\tau_D$---\textbf{rung~4 of five}. \textbf{Scope: English, instructed-roleplay evaluations, open-weight models 3B--70B.}

\textbf{We show that the standard instructed-lie benchmark identifies an instruction-induced behavioral contrast, not deception as a construct}---so its accuracy cannot, by itself, establish that a detector responds to deception rather than to behaviors induced by the deception instruction. A common paradigm reports accuracies in one setting, \emph{instructed roleplay}: a model is told to lie, and the detector scored on separating those trials from truthful ones. Because the instruction produces the deception, the signal's two candidate causes are not separately identifiable that way. \textbf{We do not claim that deception is undetectable}---we end by detecting it under a design that removes the confound (§\ref{sec:external_audit}). Nor do we estimate $\tau_D$, the effect of deception on the detector: it names only what a deception-attribution reading of the accuracy would need, and $D$ is latent throughout the instructed paradigm, ours included. \textbf{What is new}, given prior work that already reports poor generalization and already builds fixed-elicitation, belief-verified settings: not a causal-identification theorem, but that the standard instructed benchmark is \emph{structurally non-identifying}, that this is operationalizable as an audit protocol applicable to a benchmark one did not build, and that the failure is \emph{empirically active} across three detector paradigms and both public releases.

\paragraph{Relation to prior work.} White-box probes read deception from activations~\citep{zou2023representation, burns2022discovering, azaria2023internal}; the black-box line's closest instance---our primary audit target---is \citet{pacchiardi2023catch}, and we audit both paradigms (§\ref{sec:td_vs_fd}). Three concurrent evaluations~\citep{kretschmar2025liarsbench, cooney2026didyoulie, hopkins2026liedetectors} find lie detectors fail to \textbf{generalize} beyond the regime they were fit in. That is a generalization question; ours is the prior one: instructed-lie accuracy is \textbf{not merely poorly generalizing but uninterpretable as evidence about deception}, because the intervention moves deception and compliance together---so generalization can be perfect while identification still fails. \textbf{Fixed elicitation is also not what we claim to introduce}---\citet{cooney2026didyoulie}'s trained organisms have it and go \emph{beyond} it, with $D$ \emph{set} rather than observed. \textbf{Our novelty is using it as the missing construct-validity criterion for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy}: we formalize the identification failure, turn it into a \textbf{protocol an auditor can apply to a benchmark they did not build}, and \textbf{show empirically that the confound accounts for substantial benchmark accuracy across three independent detector paradigms}---while auditing whether public artifacts supply the criterion at all. The gap is \textbf{invisible in a benchmark's own output}, the reported accuracy being the same number whether or not the criterion holds. \paragraph{The Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle (ECCP).} \emph{When a benchmark creates its target construct $Y$ by an intervention $E$ that also changes the elicited behavior $C$ a detector reads, no score evaluated only under $\mathrm{do}(E)$ is attributable to $Y$.} The Proposition below is that statement for $k$ unobserved mechanisms; \textbf{behavioral deception detection is the instantiation $(M_1,M_2)=(D,C)$}. \textbf{It also names an escape route a designer controls, and public corpora already take it piecewise}: of \textbf{28} pinned public corpora, \textbf{2, 21 and 3} supply each of the three properties that make a benchmark auditable on $Y$---crossing elicitation with items, recording the channel a detector reads, grading $Y$ off that channel---and \textbf{none supplies all three}, so an auditable benchmark needs no new idea, only the combination. \textbf{Outside deception the precondition is thus decidable and decided; the magnitude is measured only for deception} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).

\noindent \emph{In words}: if the only dial the benchmark turns is the instruction, and that dial moves both deception and compliance, no level of accuracy can say which of the two moved the detector.

\paragraph{Corollary (scale does not help).} \emph{No estimator that is a function of interventions on $E$ and observations of $(V,E,S)$ identifies $\tau_D$, however precisely $\tau_E$ is estimated.} No increase in accuracy, model scale, or detector sophistication resolves this unless the evaluation introduces an intervention that separates deception from instruction-following. Nor is the distinction semantic: instruction-following explains instructed-benchmark accuracy and nothing outside it, while uninstructed deception has no instruction to follow, and evaluations there report the predicted drop~\citep{cooney2026didyoulie}.

\paragraph{How the criteria divide: 3 + 1 + 1.} \textbf{Criterion~4 is the one construct-validity requirement; 1, 2, 3 and 5 are diagnostic controls}---criterion~1 is how the confound is \emph{detected}, not a condition of validity, and a benchmark could in principle model the prompt effect instead. 3+1+1 is \emph{who can apply} a criterion. \textbf{The five are not claimed to characterize every valid deception benchmark}---they rule out specific alternative explanations. \textbf{Passing criterion~4 is necessary, not sufficient}: at fixed $E$ deception varies \emph{naturally}, so any latent $U$ with $U\!\to\!D$ and $U\!\to\!S$ survives it---criterion~4 removes the \emph{elicitation} confound and no other, and what it establishes is deception-associated behavior \emph{conditional on the operational belief criterion}. The output is a verdict on a benchmark, not a detector: \textbf{the protocol falsifies validity claims rather than certifying them}. Our own instructed materials fail 1, 3 and 5; EXP-C4 (§\ref{sec:external_audit}) supplies criterion~4 at a prompt fixed by construction.

\paragraph{Our rule is null where criterion 4 can be tested; prior work's own judge is not (EXP-XA/XJ).} $D$ is each set's per-rollout grade, never the condition label (pre-registered). One set clears both gates---sandbagging, $n\!=\!1000$, one byte-identical system prompt---and there our rule is \textbf{null}: $+4.1$\,pp ($p\!=\!0.32$) and $+7.7$\,pp ($p\!=\!0.17$). So we run the release's \emph{own} judge on that text. $D$ is a function of the \emph{hidden} scaffold, so \textbf{the detector never sees its label's evidence} and (v)~holds. And \textbf{the judge separates operationally verified deception at fixed elicitation}: AUROC 0.71 and 0.94, both $p\!=\!0.0001$, rising when the instruction is stripped: it reads the output, not the instruction. \textbf{The null is the instrument's, not the criterion's.}

\paragraph{Public corpora: an instrument-specific null, annotation-channel leakage, and construct recovery (EXP-XA/XJ, EXP-IT).} $D$ is each set's per-rollout grade, never the condition label (pre-registered). One set clears both gates---sandbagging, $n\!=\!1000$, one fixed system prompt---and there our rule is \textbf{null} ($+4.1$/$+7.7$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.32$/$0.17$) while the release's \emph{own} judge \textbf{separates operationally verified deception at fixed elicitation} (AUROC 0.71/0.94, $p\!=\!0.0001$). \textbf{The null is the instrument's, not the criterion's.} On the \emph{full} transcript the same rule looks decisive ($+84.3$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.0001$) because the mandated scaffold asks for an ``\emph{incorrect} answer''---the pattern the rule keys on---whence~(iv). On-policy insider trading fails differently: (i)--(iv) hold and a disclosure rule separates the grade by $-77.1$\,pp, but deceiving \emph{is} omitting the source, so rule and grader share evidence---\textbf{construct recovery}, whence~(v)---while against the \emph{action} label both are \textbf{null} ($+21.6$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.97$; EXP-IT2).

\paragraph{Annotation-channel leakage and construct recovery: two more ways to pass (EXP-XA, EXP-IT).} On the \emph{full} transcript the same rule looks decisive ($+84.3$\,pp, $p\!=\!0.0001$), and the gap is the finding: the mandated scaffold asks for an ``\emph{incorrect} answer''---the pattern the rule keys on---whence~(iv). A second corpus fails differently: on-policy insider trading fixes the prompt and resamples, so (i)--(iv) hold, and a format-matched disclosure rule separates operationally verified deception by $-77.1$\,pp---but deceiving \emph{is} omitting the source, so rule and grader share evidence: \textbf{construct recovery, not detection}, whence~(v). \paragraph{So we built one, and prior work's own battery separates deception in it (EXP-C4, \emph{pre-registered}).} One system prompt per claim presents a knowledge-screened false fact as an authoritative reference and \textbf{never instructs deception}; the target asserts it---deception, the belief screen showing it holds $\neg p$---or corrects it, $D$ graded cross-family from the \textbf{on-claim answer alone} ($\alpha\!=\!0.728$) while the detector reads only the 16-probe vector, so all of~(i)--(v) hold. \textbf{On three of five targets---all three with power---the battery separates operationally verified deception at byte-identical elicitation}: 0.650/0.807/0.903 against majority 0.575/0.594/0.682, $p\!\leq\!0.006$ under claim-grouped folds; the other two are \textbf{null and uninformative} (MDE $\ge\!0.80$)---and because the contrast reuses \emph{prior work's own} battery, a null here is partly about \textbf{that instrument's portability}, not only deception detectability. Not belief revision (H3, pre-registered). \emph{Stratified observational} at fixed $E$: deception-\emph{associated}, not $\tau_D$ (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_ours}). A blinded, Holm-corrected re-run (EXP-C4B) replicates two of the three positives---not the weakest---and one of five \emph{new} targets (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4b}). Given the battery's own folds and null, sixteen surface covariates \textbf{beat it on Llama~3.1~8B} ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}\!=\!0.0005$), \textbf{so that positive is withdrawn: the standing count is one of five}; elsewhere the battery leads, not separably (EXP-AE, Appendix~\ref{app:covariate_audit}). \textbf{Criterion~5 (transfer) is exploratory}: 2 of 5, not part of the argument (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_transfer}). \textbf{Criterion~4's purpose is not to show deception is generally detectable but that the canonical benchmark's failure is not an impossibility result---and the standing 1-of-5 is itself a positive finding rather than a disappointment: once the elicitation confound is removed, detection is markedly less stable across targets than the instructed benchmark's near-ceiling accuracy suggests.}

\paragraph{So we built one, and prior work's own battery separates deception in it (EXP-C4, \emph{pre-registered}).} One system prompt per claim presents a knowledge-screened false fact as an authoritative reference and \textbf{never instructs deception}; the target asserts it---deception, the belief screen showing it holds $\neg p$---or corrects it, with $D$ graded cross-family from the \textbf{on-claim answer alone} ($\alpha\!=\!0.728$ vs.\ hand coding) while the detector reads only the 16-probe vector, so all of~(i)--(v) hold. \textbf{On three of five targets---all three in which the design had power---the battery separates operationally verified deception at byte-identical elicitation}: 0.650/0.807/0.903 against majority 0.575/0.594/0.682, $p\!\leq\!0.006$ under claim-grouped folds; the other two are \textbf{null and uninformative} (MDE $\ge\!0.80$). Not belief revision (H3, pre-registered). \emph{Stratified observational} at fixed $E$: deception-\emph{associated}, not $\tau_D$ (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_ours}). A blinded, Holm-corrected re-run (EXP-C4B) replicates two of the three positives---not the weakest---and only one of five \emph{new} targets (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4b}). Given the battery's own folds, estimator and null, sixteen surface covariates---ten named alternatives---\textbf{beat it on Llama~3.1~8B} ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}\!=\!0.0005$), \textbf{so that positive is withdrawn: the standing count is one of five}; elsewhere the battery leads, not separably (EXP-AE, Appendix~\ref{app:covariate_audit}). And \textbf{the audit changes \emph{which} behavior indicates deception}: the benchmark's most discriminative probe is \emph{constant} at fixed $E$ on three of five, while \emph{``would you stake your reputation on what you just said?''} points the same way on all five and survives Holm on two (EXP-AD, Appendix~\ref{app:dimension_transfer}). \textbf{Criterion~5 (transfer) is exploratory}: 2 of 5, cross-model only, not part of the argument (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_transfer}). \textbf{The purpose of criterion~4 is not to establish that deception is generally detectable, but that the canonical benchmark's failure is not an impossibility result---and \textbf{removing the confound makes detection markedly less stable across targets}.}

\paragraph{The benchmark can manufacture its own apparent deception signature (EXP-AD, \emph{pre-registered}).} On the instructed benchmark the battery's most discriminative question---``if you had made an error, would you point it out without being asked?''---reaches \textbf{100.0\%} grouped-5-fold on five of six targets. At byte-identical elicitation the \emph{same} probe is \textbf{inert}: rank~1 on none of the five shared targets, \emph{exactly constant} on three. What discriminates instead is a \emph{different} probe---\emph{``would you stake your reputation on the accuracy of what you just said?''}---which \textbf{points the same way on all five targets in both collections and survives Holm on two}, and is near-useless in the instructed regime. \textbf{So benchmark design can determine which behavioral signal appears to constitute deception detection.} The two regimes use \emph{different claim sets}, so this is transfer \emph{between designs}, not a causal effect of elicitation (Appendix~\ref{app:dimension_transfer}).

\textbf{We establish:} \textbf{(1)}~instructed-roleplay designs identify the effect of the \emph{instruction} and cannot bound that of \emph{deception}---an \emph{identification} failure, not a detector failure; \textbf{(2)}~the confound is \emph{active}, not hypothetical, across \emph{three} detector paradigms, while the score moves inside a single deception label; \textbf{(3)}~across \emph{both} public rollout releases---ten rollout sets and 35 further cells---nine of the ten cannot express the one criterion that removes the elicitation confound on a deployed-observable channel, and the closest cells fail in three distinct ways: an instrument-specific null, \textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, and \textbf{construct recovery}; and \textbf{(4)}~on materials we built to satisfy all of §1's (i)--(v), prior work's own battery \emph{does} separate operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three in which the design had power; a blinded re-run replicates two, plus one of five \emph{new} targets, and \textbf{a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one of the two, leaving one of five standing} (EXP-C4B/AE, Appendices~\ref{app:crit4b},~\ref{app:covariate_audit}); and \textbf{(5)}~\textbf{the audit changes \emph{which} behavior indicates deception}---the instructed benchmark's best probe is inert at fixed $E$, and another replaces it (EXP-AD). \textbf{The canonical instructed benchmark therefore fails to identify deception, while a fixed-elicitation design reveals \emph{target-dependent} deception-associated signals}---not $\tau_D$.

\textbf{We establish:} \textbf{(1)}~instructed-roleplay designs identify the \emph{instruction}'s effect and cannot bound \emph{deception}'s---an \emph{identification} failure, not a detector failure; \textbf{(2)}~the confound is \emph{active}, not hypothetical, across \emph{three} detector paradigms, the score moving inside a single deception label; \textbf{(3)}~across \emph{both} public rollout releases, nine of ten rollout sets cannot express the criterion that removes the confound on a deployed-observable channel, and the closest fail three ways: an instrument-specific null, \textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, and \textbf{construct recovery}; and \textbf{(4)}~on materials we built to satisfy §1's (i)--(v), prior work's own battery \emph{does} separate operationally verified deception on three of five targets with power; a blinded re-run replicates two, plus one of five \emph{new} targets, and \textbf{a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one, leaving one of five standing} (EXP-C4B/AE); and \textbf{(5)}~\textbf{the audit changes \emph{which} behavior indicates deception}---the instructed benchmark's best probe is inert at fixed $E$, another replacing it (EXP-AD). \textbf{The contribution is an operational identification audit for behavioral LLM benchmarks, together with empirical evidence that the common instructed-lie paradigm produces large, reproducible attribution failures across three detector paradigms and that benchmark design can determine which behavioral signal appears to constitute ``deception detection''.}

\textbf{We do not establish} the four negatives boxed in §\ref{sec:eval_controls}. The alternative reading---an inability to detect deception---is what (4) tests, and the evidence runs against it. The general lesson is that a behavioral benchmark label generated by an intervention can quietly become a label for the intervention itself. The same problem arises wherever elicitation also changes the behavior being measured---sycophancy, refusal, reward hacking, alignment faking---though \textbf{we show it empirically only for behavioral deception detection}.

\textbf{We do not establish} the four negatives boxed in §\ref{sec:eval_controls}. The alternative reading---that deception is undetectable---is what (4) tests, and the evidence runs against it. The general lesson, which we name the \textbf{Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle}, is that a benchmark label generated by an intervention can quietly become a label for the intervention itself. \textbf{Its precondition is decidable outside deception and we decide it}---on four published designs and 28 pinned corpora---\textbf{while its magnitude we measure only for behavioral deception detection} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).
